questions.q: Why do LSM-tree storage engines handle heavy write loads well?
options: Writes go to memory and an append-only log, deferring sorted-file merges
They update rows in place, avoiding any write amplification
They automatically shard every incoming write across all disks in the machine
They skip the write-ahead log, halving the I/O per insert

questions.q: Compared with LSM trees, what is a B-tree engine's typical strength?
options: Much faster sustained ingestion of random writes at very high data volumes
Lower disk usage because pages never fragment
Efficient point reads and range scans without merging multiple files
No need for background maintenance processes

questions.q: What is downsampling in a time-series database?
options: Dropping every record older than the retention window immediately
Replacing old raw points with lower-resolution aggregates like 5-minute rollups
Sampling a fraction of incoming writes to reduce the ingest load
Compressing timestamps by storing deltas instead of absolutes

questions.q: What does a retention policy in a time-series store control?
options: Which users may query each measurement and tag
How database replicas resynchronize after a temporary network partition
The maximum cardinality allowed per tag key
How long data is kept before automatic expiry or deletion

questions.q: In time-series data models, what is 'tag cardinality'?
options: The number of data points stored per series each second
The number of distinct values a tag key can take across series
The maximum count of tag keys permitted on any single measurement
The ratio of tags to fields in each written point

questions.q: Why are time-series writes considered append-friendly?
options: Points are keyed randomly, spreading writes evenly across pages
Old points are rewritten each time a newer point arrives
Each incoming write updates an aggregate row in place
New points mostly carry recent timestamps, extending the series' end

questions.q: What is a common first-line technique to survive write spikes to a time-series store?
options: Synchronous writes straight to the storage nodes for durability
Read replicas that absorb the extra write traffic
Buffering through a message queue that smooths bursts
Doubling the retention period so data spreads over more disk

questions.q: Which compression trick exploits the shape of typical metric data?
options: Delta-of-delta timestamps and XOR-encoded float values
Dictionary-encoding each measurement name per data point
Encrypting repeated values so they deduplicate in storage
Row-level gzip applied independently to every point

questions.q: Ingest slows and read latency spikes while background disk I/O is saturated on an LSM store. What is the likely cause?
options: The WAL is replaying because a replica restarted
B-tree page splits are cascading through the index
Compaction is falling behind, piling up SSTables and read amplification
The block cache keeps evicting hot pages because of large scans

questions.q: You add request_id as a tag on every metric point. Weeks later the TSDB's memory explodes. Why?
options: Each unique tag value creates a new series, and series indexes live in memory
Tag values are stored uncompressed on disk, roughly doubling the footprint of every point
request_id values collide across shards, forcing constant rebalancing
High-frequency writes bypass the buffer and fragment the WAL

questions.q: Partitioning a metrics table by metric_name sends 40% of traffic to one node. Which repartitioning usually fixes this?
options: Partition by ingestion server hostname instead of the metric
Partition by metric_name plus a random suffix on every write
Move the hot metric to its own dedicated cluster permanently
Partition by a composite of series key and time bucket

questions.q: Queries for 'last 5 minutes' dashboards are fast, but 90-day trend queries crush the cluster. Which design addresses the trend queries?
options: Increase scrape frequency so trends need fewer points
Precomputed rollups at hourly resolution queried instead of raw data
A much larger block cache dedicated to holding raw historical blocks
Query-time sampling that reads every tenth raw point

questions.q: Why does time-based partitioning (one partition per day) make retention cheap?
options: Old rows compress better once the partition is a day old
Queries never touch old partitions, so deletes are invisible
Each daily partition maintains its own write-ahead log that expires automatically
Expiry becomes dropping whole partitions instead of row-by-row deletes

questions.q: A write-heavy IoT platform sees 10x write amplification on a B-tree store. What mostly drives that amplification?
options: Foreign-key checks executed for every single inserted reading
Random-key inserts dirtying and rewriting many pages plus index updates
Compaction rewriting SSTables at each level of the tree
Timestamps stored as strings inflating each row's size

questions.q: Dashboard queries using regex over metric names are slow at high series counts. What's the underlying reason?
options: Regex matching must scan the series index rather than seek exact keys
Regex forces the store to decompress every data block fully
The query planner serializes all regex queries onto one thread
Metric names are hashed, so regex requires rebuilding names from hashes

questions.q: You must keep raw data 7 days, 1-minute rollups 90 days, hourly rollups 2 years. What implements this cleanly?
options: One table with a TTL column checked by every query
Client-side filtering that ignores data past each horizon
Tiered retention policies with continuous or scheduled aggregation jobs
Nightly exports of old raw data into CSV archives kept on object storage

questions.q: An LSM store shows fast writes but p99 reads degrade over weeks. Compaction is keeping up. What subtler cause fits?
options: The WAL has grown past the operating system's page cache size
Bloom filters and indexes for many levels no longer fit in memory
Tombstones from TTL deletes are pinned in level zero forever
Timestamp compression breaks once epochs exceed 32 bits

questions.q: Sizing: 200k devices send one 100-byte point every 10 seconds. Roughly what sustained write rate must the cluster absorb?
options: About 20k points/sec, roughly 2 MB/sec before replication
About 2k points/sec, roughly 200 KB/sec before replication
About 200k points/sec, roughly 20 MB/sec before replication
About 1.2M points/sec, roughly 120 MB/sec before replication

questions.q: A multi-tenant TSDB lets one tenant register unbounded tag values, degrading everyone. Which control is most effective?
options: Per-tenant rate limits on write requests per second
Per-tenant disk usage quotas enforced strictly at the storage layer
Per-tenant series-cardinality limits enforced at ingestion
Per-tenant query timeouts that kill expensive scans

questions.q: Writes arrive mostly in time order, but 2% are days late (device backfill). Why do very late writes hurt LSM/TSDB performance disproportionately?
options: Late points must be encrypted separately from their block
The WAL must be replayed from the late point's timestamp forward
Late points force the query planner to disable index usage
They land in already-compacted or sealed time blocks, forcing rewrites or overlaps
